events.name: The Bathhouse at the Edge of Night

remembers.notice: The Indeedee leans in and sniffs your sleeve: fried dough, burnt sugar, something sold on a stick at a festival stall. Its nose wrinkles. "Not here, you don't."

events.intro: At dusk you come to a river you have crossed before, and there is a bridge over it that was not there this morning. It is red, and old, and dry, though the river is high. On the far side: lanterns, a long tiled roof, steam rolling off it into the dark. You are halfway over before you decide to be. At the door stands an Indeedee in a starched apron, holding a ledger. "You're early. Or you're human. Either way, you'll have to work." It turns a page. "Guests here are spirits. They come to wash off the day. Some of them have very long days." It looks at you over the ledger. "Work until dawn and you can cross back. Don't eat the food."

success.text: The Indeedee does not smile, but it writes something in the ledger, and when you read it upside down it is your name. It hands you an apron that fits exactly. Behind it, the whole bathhouse breathes out steam, like something that has been waiting for you.

You turn round. There is no bridge. There is the river, wide and black, and the far bank where you stood a minute ago, very small and very far. Behind you the Indeedee waits without hurrying, as if this happens every night. It probably does.

choices.label: What happens if I eat the food?

success.text: The Indeedee closes the ledger on one finger, to keep its place, and gives the question its full attention.

events.name: Sleeves Up
events.intro: The Indeedee walks fast and talks faster. Corridors of steam, paper doors, the smell of cedar and hot stone. Shapes pass you in the mist with towels over their shoulders. "Three shifts. The big tub on the lower floor: a guest came in muddy and it is getting worse. Then the tea room. Then the front desk: somebody has lost their name, and it is upsetting the others." It stops at a door that is shaking slightly on its runners. "Start here."

success.text: You roll them up. The Indeedee watches, approves of the second fold and not the first, and slides the door open. A wave of brown, cold air rolls out over your shoes.

events.name: No Bridge
events.intro: The Indeedee comes and stands beside you and looks at the place where the bridge was. "It comes at dusk and goes when someone is inside. It comes back at dawn." It does not say "I told you." It holds out an apron, folded in four. "Everybody who tries to leave says they are not staying. Then they work. Then they cross back. It is a good system. It has never once failed."

success.text: It fits exactly, which is the strangest thing so far. The Indeedee is already walking. "The big tub first. Sleeves up. Mind the step: it is older than you."

events.name: The Way Back
events.intro: "You forget the way back," says the Indeedee. It does not lower its voice. It is not a threat. It is a fact, the way the river being wet is a fact. "Guests eat. Guests are already where they are going. You are not." Somewhere inside a gong sounds, and the smell of something sweet and fried drifts past. Your stomach answers it out loud. The Indeedee pretends not to hear. "Now. Will you work?"

success.text: It nods once, writes your name in the ledger and hands you an apron. "Good. The big tub first. And if a guest offers you a dumpling, you are allergic."
You glance back over your shoulder. There is no bridge. There is only the river, black and wide. "It comes back at dawn," says the Indeedee, and hands you an apron, folded in four. "Everyone works."

events.name: The River Guest

remembers.notice: The guest lifts its head. Under the mud, two eyes open, and they know you. You waded into it once this run, with bin bags and gloves, and pulled things out of it. It sighs, a long river sigh, and some of the mud simply slides off by itself.

addChoices.label: Pick up where you left off.

success.text: It leans into the brush like an old dog. The mud comes away in sheets. Under it: a bicycle, a fridge, and, wound round and round with fishing line in the very middle, a small Feebas that has been holding its breath for a long time. You cut the line. It slips away into the guest, which is clear water now, clear to the stones. The guest stands, shakes itself, and leaves on the tiles one pellet of clean grey silt. Then it is gone, and somewhere below you hear water running fast and clean.

remembers.notice: The guest smells of a factory pipe, but the smell is old. It lifts its head and looks at you, and you understand that the pipe is cold now. You are the one who shut it. It sighs, and some of the mud simply slides off by itself.

addChoices.label: Pick up where you left off.

success.text: It leans into the brush like an old dog. The mud comes away in sheets. Under it: a bicycle, a fridge, and, wound round and round with fishing line in the very middle, a small Feebas that has been holding its breath for a long time. You cut the line. It slips away into the guest, which is clear water now, clear to the stones. The guest stands, shakes itself, and leaves on the tiles one pellet of clean grey silt. Then it is gone, and somewhere below you hear water running fast and clean.

events.intro: The lower floor is one enormous wooden tub, and in it sits a guest so caked in mud you cannot tell what shape it is. A Ghost-type, you think, from the cold coming off it. It is also, somehow, a river. Brown water runs off it and does not stop. It smells of drains and diesel and old weed. It does not look at you. It looks very tired of being looked at. "Scrub," says the Indeedee from the door. "Hard. It will not mind. It will not say thank you either."

success.text: You put your back into it, and it gives. Under the mud: a bicycle. You haul it out. A fridge. A trolley wheel. And in the very middle, wound round and round with fishing line, a small Feebas that has been holding its breath for a very long time. You cut the line. It slips away into the guest, which is clear water now, clear to the stones. The guest stands, shakes itself, and leaves on the tiles one pellet of clean grey silt. Then it is gone, and somewhere far below you hear water running fast and clean.

failure.text: The mud fights back. It gets in your hair, your ears, your lead Pokémon's fur. It takes all night that you have, and some you do not. But a bicycle comes out, and a fridge, and at last, tangled in fishing line, a small Feebas, which you cut free. The guest stands up clear to the stones and leaves you one pellet of clean grey silt. You and your lead are wrung out.

success.text: Your Water-type climbs into the tub as if it owned it and starts to churn. The river guest goes very still, then leans in: it has not felt clean water against it for years. The mud lifts in clouds. Out comes a bicycle, a fridge, and a small Feebas wound in fishing line, which you cut free. The guest stands, clear as glass, and leaves one pellet of clean grey silt on the tiles. Your Water-type does not want to get out.

events.name: The Fussiest Cup
events.intro: The tea room is low tables and paper lanterns, and every cup on the shelf is a Sinistea. Most of them are asleep. One is not. It sits in a chipped antique cup with a crack in the glaze, and it has opinions. The water is too hot. Now it is too cold. That leaf is the wrong leaf. A guest in a grey shawl has been waiting an hour for it to agree to be poured. "This one," says the Indeedee, "is very old, and very fussy, and very good. Serve the guest."

choices.label: Let it steep as long as it likes.

success.text: You sit down on the floor and wait. So does the guest. It takes a long time. When the Sinistea finally tips itself and pours, the tea is the colour of a sunset and smells of rain on a hot road. The guest drinks with both hands and closes its eyes. Over the rim of its cup, the Sinistea watches you. It has decided something about you.

choices.label: Ask it how it wants to be poured.

success.text: Nobody has asked it before. It rattles, startled, then rattles in a different, more particular way, and you work it out between you: the left hand, the third cushion, the kettle just off the boil, a small bow first. The tea is perfect. The guest weeps a little and does not say why. The old Sinistea looks very pleased with itself, and with you.

It is not happy. It sloshes. The tea is fine, more or less, and the guest is too tired to mind. But the old Sinistea turns its cup so the crack faces you, which the Indeedee tells you later is the worst thing a teacup can do to a person.

events.name: The Guest Without a Name
events.intro: At the front desk a guest is standing very still. It is pale and thin as steam and has no face to speak of, and the other guests step round it uneasily. "It came in with the others and signed nothing," the Indeedee says quietly. "Now it cannot remember what it is called. Without a name it cannot leave. Without leaving, it starts to fade." The guest turns toward you. Something in it is listening very hard. "Find it. Before dawn."

success.text: Page after page of names in a hundred hands. Near the bottom of one page is only a smudge, as if someone began to write and was called away. You hold it to the lantern. Under the smudge, pressed into the paper: four letters. You read them out loud. The guest flickers hard, like a candle in a doorway, and then it has a face. It is smiling, and it is much younger than you thought.

"Water," it whispers, if steam can whisper. "A bridge. Somebody calling me in for supper." You ask what they called. It does not know. You ask what the somebody sounded like. "Like you," it says, and slowly it says its own name back in your voice, and hears it. It has a face again. It is somebody's child, who wandered off a long time ago and has worked here ever since, waiting to be called in.

The guests are shy, and then they are not. One remembers it sat by the window. One remembers it always took the last bath. Then the old Sinistea from the tea room rattles across the floor in its cup and says, very firmly, a single word. Everyone goes quiet. The guest straightens. That was it. That was its name. The Sinistea looks at you as if you owe it one.

events.name: The Bridge at Dawn

remembers.notice: The old Sinistea still has its crack turned toward you. It has not forgiven the pouring. It is, however, still sitting on the step.

success.text: "I was in a hurry. I'm sorry." It thinks about this for a long, long time. Then it turns round, tips toward you a fraction, and lets you carry it, very carefully, over the bridge. It will take a while to forgive you properly. It has time. Teacups always do. Behind you the lanterns go out one by one.

effects.text: You worked a night in the bathhouse at the edge of night, and came back over the bridge at dawn with a teacup that had opinions.

remembers.notice: The Indeedee glances at your hands, then at your mouth. "You didn't eat." It nods, once. From an Indeedee, that is a medal.

events.intro: Grey light at the paper windows. The steam thins. The Indeedee takes your apron, folds it in four and puts it on a shelf with a great many others. "Dawn. The bridge is back." It walks you to the door. The river guest's pellet is in your pocket, still warm. On the step, in its chipped antique cup, sits the old Sinistea from the tea room. It has its back to you, very pointedly, in the way of something that wants to be asked.

choices.label: Ask the cup to come with you.

success.text: You crouch and ask. It turns round slowly, as if it had only just noticed you. It rattles, very particularly: left hand, third pocket, not too fast. You carry it out over the bridge exactly so. Behind you the lanterns go out one by one. The Indeedee does not wave. When you look back from the far bank there is no bridge, only morning on the river, running clean.

effects.text: You worked a night in the bathhouse at the edge of night, and came back over the bridge at dawn with a teacup that had opinions.

choices.label: Leave it with its tea room.

success.text: You bow to it, the way you saw the guests do. It turns round. It bows back, a little, which costs a cup a great deal. The Indeedee presses a twist of tea leaves into your hand for the road, the good ones, the ones the old cup lets nobody else touch. You brew them on the far bank. Your whole team sleeps like stones. When you look back there is no bridge.

effects.text: You worked a night in the bathhouse at the edge of night, and crossed back at dawn.

events.name: The Spore Doctor

remembers.notice: At your belt, the guide's bell from the fog stirs on its own. Its note goes out into the village and meets the ringing halfway. For one long breath both sounds stand still. Then they fold into each other and are gone. Along the street, one by one, people take their hands from their ears.

success.text: You hold it up and let it ring once more. The silence after is soft and whole. The villagers fall asleep where they sit, on doorsteps and benches, smiling like children. Under the trees the Morelull glow on, singing to nobody, unharmed. The doctor stares at your bell for a long time. "I have walked a long way," he says, "and I have never seen that." He writes it down in a small book.

events.intro: The village is awake at noon and has been awake all night. People sit on their doorsteps with their hands over their ears. "Can you hear it?" a woman asks you. When you say no, she starts to cry: nobody from outside ever can. A man in a long coat sits on the well with a wooden box on his back, listening with his eyes shut. "It isn't a curse. It's a spore. It lives in sound." He points at the woods, where something glows soft and blue under the trees. "It's not cruel. It just doesn't know we're here. Things like this never do." He opens his eyes. "I can drive it out or move it somewhere it won't bother anyone. Help me decide."

success.text: He nods and does not argue. He takes a lamp from his box and walks into the woods, and you go with him. Under the trees a colony of Morelull glows blue in a ring, swaying, singing a note nobody in the village asked to hear. He sets the lamp down among them. The fire takes them quickly. The ringing stops all at once, and the whole village sighs in its sleep. The doctor does not speak for an hour. When he does, it is only: "That was the right thing. It usually is. I still don't like it."

He almost smiles. From his box he takes a glass jar as big as a lantern. Under the trees the Morelull colony glows in a ring, swaying, and he coaxes them in one by one with a low hum, until the jar is full of soft light and the ringing is inside it, muffled, like a bell under a blanket. He puts it in your arms. "There's a cave three hops down the road. Dark, wet, nobody to hear. Carry it gently. It will sing the whole way."

He looks at you for a long moment. Then he goes from door to door with you and tells them what it is. He shows them the colony glowing under the trees, small and harmless, swaying as it sings. A child says it sounds like a lullaby if you stop being cross with it. That night the village sleeps for the first time in a week, with the ringing all round them. On the well, the doctor smiles. It is the first time he has. It changes his whole face.

events.name: The Jar That Sings
events.intro: Three hops down the road, as he said, a cave opens in the hillside: dark, wet, quiet as the inside of a shell. The jar has sung the whole way. It has grown warmer, too, and once when you stumbled it went very dim, and only brightened again when you said sorry to it out loud. Inside the cave the dark is total, except for you and the jar of soft blue light in your arms.

choices.label: Set the jar down in the dark.

success.text: You unscrew the lid. The Morelull pour out across the wet stone like spilled light. They find the walls and climb them, and in a minute the whole cave is a blue sky full of small swaying stars. The ringing goes up into the rock and comes back changed: a hum, a hush. Out on the road it fades to nothing. One Morelull stays on the rim of the empty jar, looking at you, until you leave.

You do not know the song, so you hum anything. The jar brightens. When you open the lid the colony pours out slowly, as if it would like to stay with you a little longer. They climb the walls and turn the cave into a night sky. The ringing goes up into the rock and comes back as a hush. One Morelull sits on your shoe and will not get off until you set it down by the others, gently.

events.name: A Coat at the End of the Road
events.intro: Days on, on a long straight road, you see a coat at the far end of it. A long coat with a wooden box on its back, walking away from you at a steady, patient pace, the pace of someone who has walked every road in every region and expects to walk them again. You would know it anywhere. The spore doctor has not seen you yet.

success.text: You run. He hears you coming and stops, and does not seem surprised. "I wondered if you would." He is on his way to a farm where a Paras has stopped moving. "Come and help me decide again. You were good at it."

You raise a hand. At the far end of the road, without turning round, he raises his. Then the road bends, and he is gone. You have a feeling he will turn up again. The roads are not as many as they look.

events.name: The Paras in the Barn
events.intro: A farm at the edge of a wood. In the barn, on a bed of straw, lies a Paras whose mushrooms have grown so big it cannot stand. The farmer's daughter sits beside it with her knees pulled up. "It was fine in the spring." The doctor kneels in the straw. "The mushroom is doing what mushrooms do. It doesn't know the Paras is there." He looks up at you. "I can cut them back, and they'll grow again. Or I can let it change into what it was always going to be. Help me decide."

success.text: He works with a small silver knife, slowly, the way you would cut someone's hair. The Paras stands up on its little legs, wobbles, and walks straight into the girl's lap. "Every spring," the doctor tells her. "Not too much. Not too little. You'll learn." She is already learning. She is watching his hands.

"Then we wait," he says, and you wait, all three of you, in the straw. Near dawn the Paras shivers. The mushrooms open like a coat, and something larger stands up in the barn: a Parasect, slow and calm and not hurting any more. The girl cries. The doctor puts a hand on her shoulder and says nothing at all, which is exactly right.

"I want it to stay my Paras," she says. Then, smaller: "But I don't want it to hurt." The doctor smiles at you over her head. He cuts them back a little, shows her how, and leaves her the silver knife. "Next spring it's your decision. You're the one who knows it."

events.name: It Glows When Something Is Wrong

remembers.notice: "It was in my box when I got back to the road," he says. "From the colony we burned. One got away, and it came to me, of all people." He does not say what he could not do then. He does not have to.
"It followed the empty jar out of the cave," he says. "All that way down the road, on its own. It must have liked how you carried it."
"The village sent it after me," he says. "Wrapped in a scarf, with a note. The note says it sings them to sleep, and they can spare one."

events.intro: Dusk, at the edge of a dark wood. The doctor is waiting where the road goes in, as if you had arranged to meet. He swings the box off his back and opens it. Inside, on a bed of moss, sits a single Morelull, glowing a slow, steady blue. As you step nearer the wood, it flares bright, and the trees beyond go quiet. "It glows when something is wrong," he says. "Something is wrong in there. Something always is." He holds the box out to you. "It should be with someone who walks into places. I mostly walk past them."

success.text: It climbs out of the box onto your shoulder and dims to a soft, pleased glow. The doctor shuts the empty box and settles it on his back. "It will warn you. Listen to it." Then he walks into the dark wood alone. The Morelull flares once, and when nothing happens, settles. Every now and then, for the rest of the run, at the far end of some road, you see a long coat.

effects.text: A spore doctor in a long coat gave you a Morelull that glows when something is wrong.

choices.label: Walk into the wood with him (a node).

success.text: The Morelull rides on your shoulder and you go in together: the doctor, you and the light. Something is wrong in there, a pool gone sour, a nest of Foongus spitting at nothing. He sees to it. You hold the light. On the far side of the wood he says, "You keep it. You'll need it more than me," and walks on. Every now and then, at the far end of some road, you see a long coat.

effects.text: You walked into a dark wood beside the spore doctor, and came out with a Morelull that glows when something is wrong.

events.name: The Book of Names
events.intro: Night, a house at the end of a lane, and a man in a damp coat waiting on the step with a key. "You're the one in the will." You have never heard of her. He has never heard of you. The will is very clear. Inside, under a dust sheet, stands a grandmother's writing desk, and in its drawer lies a book bound in grey cloth: a hundred and eight names, each in a different hand, and some of the hands are not hands at all. Something scratches at the window. A Shuppet hangs outside the glass, tapping it with its little horn. Words come up on the pane in frost, like a subtitle: GIVE ME MY NAME BACK. SHE TOOK IT IN A GAME. I LOST. The book grows warm in your lap. It glows on one page.

success.text: You find the page: one name in a scratchy, eager hand, with a little drawing of a horn under it. You tear it out along the stitching, open the window, and blow on it. The page comes apart into ash that sparkles, and the Shuppet breathes it in. It grows a shade brighter. It loops the room twice, fast, the way a dog runs when it is let off the lead. Then it presses its face to your cheek, cold as a window. THANK YOU, says the frost on the glass, in big wobbly letters. Then it is gone. The book is lighter by one page. A hundred and seven to go.

effects.text: You tore a page out of a dead stranger's book and gave a Shuppet back its name.

success.text: You close the book. The glow goes out. Outside, the Shuppet goes very still. Then slowly, as if pulled on a string, it comes through the glass and settles at your shoulder. It has to. The book says so. It will not look at you. When you walk, it follows exactly one step behind, the way a prisoner walks.

The frost on the window clears and writes again, slower: SHE WAS LONELY. SHE BEAT EVERYONE. THEN SHE HAD NO ONE LEFT TO PLAY WITH. The Shuppet stops tapping. For a moment it only looks at the desk, the way you look at a chair someone used to sit in.

events.name: The Book of Names
events.intro: The house is very quiet. The book is still warm in your hands and still glowing on one page, and the Shuppet is still at the glass. It has stopped scratching. It is waiting to see what kind of person inherits a book like this one.

success.text: You tear the page out along the stitching and blow it through the open window. The Shuppet breathes in the sparkling ash and grows a shade brighter. It loops the room twice, fast, then presses its cold face to your cheek. "She wasn't bad," the frost writes, very small. "Just alone." Then it is gone, and the book is lighter by one page.

effects.text: You tore a page out of a dead stranger's book and gave a Shuppet back its name.

success.text: You close the book. Slowly, as if pulled on a string, the Shuppet comes through the glass and settles at your shoulder. It has to. It will not look at you. When you walk, it follows exactly one step behind.

events.name: The One Who Hid Too Well
events.intro: A new region, a camp at night. You wake because the book is warm against your back through the bag. Sitting on your bedroll, very small, is a Duskull, holding up one bony finger as if it is counting to a hundred. Frost writes on the inside of your lantern: SHE FOUND ME EVERY TIME. NOBODY ELSE EVER FOUND ME. I BET HER MY NAME SHE COULDN'T FIND THAT. The Duskull stops counting. It has been hiding for sixty years, and it is tired. The book glows on one page.

success.text: You tear out the page and blow on it. The Duskull breathes the ash in, and its one red eye goes bright. It darts behind your bag, then behind a tree, then behind you, and you find it every time, and every time it shakes with something that is clearly laughing. Then it is gone into the dark, still hiding, happily, from nobody in particular.

You close the book. The Duskull goes still, and then it trails after you, because it has to. It hides behind your heel in every fight. For a while it even fights for you, hard and joyless, the way you work for a boss you do not like.

effects.label: A spirit bound by the book

success.text: You find the Duskull's page, and then you find the Shuppet's, and you tear them out together. The Shuppet at your shoulder goes stiff. You blow. Two clouds of sparkling ash. The Duskull is gone at once. The Shuppet breathes its name in and turns to you, and for the first time it looks you in the face. It could go anywhere now. It stays. It moves round from behind you to beside you, and it stays there.

events.name: The Riddle She Never Answered
events.intro: Another region, another night, and singing outside your tent: a Misdreavus, circling the lantern. Frost writes on the canvas: SHE ASKED ME ONE RIDDLE I COULD NOT ANSWER. I HAVE BEEN THINKING ABOUT IT FOR SIXTY YEARS. WHAT CAN YOU ONLY KEEP BY GIVING IT AWAY? It sounds tired. It sounds like it would very much like to stop thinking about it now. The book glows on one page.

success.text: You tear out the page and hold it up, and before you blow you say, "This." The Misdreavus goes quiet. It looks at the page, and at you, and its whole body rings like a glass somebody has tapped. That was the answer. A name is only yours while someone else will say it back. You blow. It breathes in its name and sings all the way to the trees, a new song.

You close the book. The singing stops in the middle of a note. The Misdreavus drifts down and follows you, silent, and for a while it fights for you, because it has to. It never finds out the answer to the riddle. You never tell it.

effects.label: A spirit bound by the book

success.text: You tear out the Misdreavus's page and the Shuppet's together. "This," you say to the Misdreavus, and it understands, and rings like a tapped glass. You blow. The Misdreavus sings off into the trees. The Shuppet breathes its own name in and turns and looks at you properly, for the first time. It could go anywhere. It moves round from behind you to beside you, and it stays.

events.name: The Doll She Won at Cards
events.intro: Another region. At night someone is dealing cards on your bedroll, very badly, with stitched hands. A Banette. It lays down a hand and waits for you to play. Frost writes on the back of every card: SHE WON ME AT CARDS. I WAS SOMEONE'S DOLL ONCE. THEN I WAS HERS. THEN SHE WAS GONE AND I WAS NOBODY'S. The zip on its mouth is shut tight. The book glows on one page.

success.text: You play one hand with it first, and lose, and it unzips its mouth very slightly, which on a Banette is a grin. Then you tear out the page and blow on it. It breathes its name in and holds its own stitched hands together, the way somebody once held them. It deals you one last card, face down, and is gone. The card is blank. You keep it anyway.

You close the book. It gathers its cards with great care and follows you, because it has to, and it fights for you for a while with its mouth zipped tight. It still deals a hand every night. It never asks you to play again.

effects.label: A spirit bound by the book

success.text: You tear out the Banette's page and the Shuppet's together. You blow. The Banette breathes its name in and holds its own hands. The Shuppet breathes its name in and, for the first time, looks straight at you. It could go anywhere. It comes round from behind you to beside you, and it stays.

events.name: Everyone She Beat

remembers.notice: Some of the faces are dimmer than the others. They are the ones whose pages you kept. They came anyway.

events.intro: Night. The book opens by itself, past all the torn stitching, to the very last page. It is blank. The lantern dims. One by one they come out of the dark: the Shuppet, the Duskull, the Misdreavus, the Banette, and behind them more, dozens, faces you have never seen, everyone she ever played and beat. They draw together, closer and closer, until they are one thing: a ring of faces in a cracked old stone. A Spiritomb. Frost writes on every surface at once: SHE BEAT US ALL. THEN THERE WAS NOBODY LEFT TO PLAY. WE CAME BACK TO TELL HER IT WAS ALL RIGHT. WE ARE TOO LATE. YOU WILL DO.

success.text: You sit down across from the stone. Every face in it leans in. It has waited a long time for somebody to play.

win.text: Everyone the old woman ever beat came back as one Spiritomb, played you one last game, and came with you.

lose.text: Everyone the old woman ever beat came back as one Spiritomb, won one last game at last, and came with you.

choices.label: Write her name on the last page.

success.text: You know it from the will. You write it on the blank page, in your own hand, carefully. The faces in the stone go quiet, and then, one by one, they smile. It was the only name nobody ever won from her. Now it is in the book with theirs. The Spiritomb settles at your feet like an old dog by a fire, and when you walk on, it comes.

effects.text: You wrote a lonely old woman's name in her own book, beside everyone she ever beat, and they came with you as one.

success.text: You close the book and set it on the stone. The faces look at it, and at you, and they understand. The Spiritomb sinks slowly into the ground under the trees, book and all, the way a stone settles in a riverbed. In the morning there is a small cairn there, and a feeling in your whole team of having been thanked.

effects.text: Everyone the old woman ever beat came back as one Spiritomb, and you let them rest together.

events.name: The Witch's Courier
events.intro: Something comes down out of the sky at the wrong angle and goes straight into a hedge. Parcels burst out of it in every direction. A Wattrel lands on the hedge top and squawks at the hole, very loudly, as if this has happened before. Out of the hole climbs a girl in a black dress, with leaves in her hair and a broom in two pieces. "I just started. I'm not very good at landing." She picks up a parcel, then another. Her hands are shaking. "I've lost my flying. It just stopped. I don't know why." She looks at the scattered parcels, then at you. "Can you help me deliver these? On foot? I'll pay you in cake."

success.text: Her whole face changes. She stuffs the parcels into your arms and hers, three of them with addresses in careful round writing. "This one's the lighthouse. This one's the boy on Mill Street. This one's a lady who only moved here last week." The Wattrel lands on her head and stays there, like a hat that disapproves. "One at a time. Along your way. Thank you. Thank you."

She sits down on the kerb with the broken broom across her knees. "Because I started wondering whether I should be doing this at all." She says it very quietly, as if it might hear. "You can't fly and wonder that at the same time. It turns out."

The Wattrel looks at you as if you have said something rude. "It can't," she says. "It only flies with me. When I stopped, it stopped too." The Wattrel hops down onto her shoulder and stays very close against her neck, and does not fly anywhere at all.

events.name: The Witch's Courier
events.intro: The girl is still sitting on the kerb, with the broken broom across her knees and the Wattrel tucked against her neck. The parcels are stacked beside her in a careful, hopeful pile. "So. Will you help? It's three. They're not heavy. The cake is very good."

success.text: "Really?" She is on her feet at once. She stuffs the parcels into your arms: the lighthouse, the boy on Mill Street, the lady who only moved here last week. "One at a time. Along your way. Thank you."

She nods as if she expected it, and gathers the parcels up herself. As you go you look back once. She is walking, very carefully, with the broom under her arm and the Wattrel on her head, toward the first address.

events.name: The Lighthouse
events.intro: The first parcel goes to the lighthouse. The keeper opens the door before you knock: he has watched you come the whole way along the sea wall. He is lonely the way people are when everyone they love is far away and doing well. The parcel is soft. Inside is a jumper his daughter knitted, a little too big, with a note that says she is sorry she can't come this year either.

choices.label: Stay for a cup of tea.

success.text: He makes tea in two cups that have not both been used for a long time. He tells you about his daughter, who is clever and far away. He puts the jumper on over his other jumper and does not take it off. When you leave he is reading the note again, smiling, and he waves from the top of the light.
He takes it with both hands. "From my girl," he says, to you, to the sea, to nobody. You leave him holding it against his chest at the top of the steps.

events.name: Mill Street
events.intro: The second parcel goes to a boy on Mill Street. He is lonely the way children are when their best friend has moved away and the street has gone quiet. The parcel rattles. Inside is a board game for two players, and a card from the friend that says: YOU HAVE TO FIND SOMEONE TO PLAY WITH. THOSE ARE THE RULES.

success.text: You lose. He wins with enormous dignity and explains every rule twice. By the end, two other kids from the street are watching over the fence. He sets the board up again for them before you have left the gate.
He reads the card three times. Then he looks up and down the empty street, takes a deep breath, and goes and knocks on the door next to his own. You do not stay to see who opens it.

events.name: The New Lady
events.intro: The last parcel goes to a flat above a shop, to a woman who moved to the town last week. She is lonely the way people are in a crowd: everyone is busy, everyone is kind, and nobody knows her name. The parcel is from her own mother, from home. It is a jar of the jam she grew up on, wrapped in a tea towel that smells of the house.

success.text: She tells you. She says it twice, as if she had nearly forgotten what it sounded like out loud. She opens the jam right there on the stairs and you both eat some off one spoon. On your way out, the shopkeeper downstairs asks who she is, and you tell him. You hear him say it to her as you go: good morning, and her name.
She holds the jar to her face and breathes in through the tea towel, and her eyes fill. "It smells like the kitchen," she says. You leave her on the stairs with it.

events.name: Paid in Cake
events.intro: The girl is waiting where you left her, sitting on the kerb with a cake box on her knees. "Did they like them? Were they all right?" You tell her about the lighthouse, and Mill Street, and the lady above the shop. She listens to every word with her chin on the box. "Everyone's lonely in a different way," she says. "I never noticed. I was always too high up." She hands you the cake. It is very good.

success.text: She thinks about that for a long time. Then she picks up the mended broom and holds it, not to fly, only to hold it. "See you round, courier," she says, and the Wattrel squawks, once, like a full stop.

events.name: The Clock Tower
events.intro: Three stages on, in another town, there is a little shop with a hand-painted sign: DELIVERIES, ON FOOT. The girl is behind the counter. The broom leans in the corner, mended. "It still doesn't fly. I try every morning. I get about an inch." She points out of the window at the clock tower, where a boy in overalls is hanging off the clock face with a spanner. "That's Tobin. He fixes the clock. He says I'm the best courier in town because I actually knock." The Wattrel is asleep in the parcel tray.

choices.label: Hold the broom steady for her.

success.text: Out in the yard you hold the end of the broom while she sits on it. It wobbles. It rises an inch, then two, then a whole hand. She laughs out loud, and then she stops laughing to look down, and it drops. But it rose.

failure.text: It wobbles, and you wobble, and the two of you go into the shop's own hedge together, which she says is a sign. She is laughing anyway. "Every morning," she says, picking leaves out of your hair. "Every morning, an inch."

choices.label: Tell her she doesn't have to fly.

success.text: She goes very still. Then she puts her face in her hands and her shoulders shake, and when she looks up she is smiling. "Nobody's said that. Everyone says I'll get it back." She wipes her eyes on the cuff of her dress. "I might not. That's all right. I like knocking on doors."

choices.label: Eat cake with her and Tobin.

success.text: Tobin climbs down for it. He eats like somebody who works on top of a tower, which is to say fast and without sitting down. He talks about gears. She watches him talk, and the way she watches him is something she has not noticed yet. You notice. You do not say.

events.name: She Has to Fly

remembers.notice: She looks past you at the street. The lighthouse keeper is there in his too-big jumper. The boy from Mill Street is there with half the street behind him. The lady from above the shop is there, holding her umbrella over strangers. They all came to watch her. They are all looking up.

success.text: You say nothing. She does not need you to. She grabs the street sweeper's broom off its hook, because hers is at the shop, and she kicks off, and she flies. Not well. Fast and crooked and furious, into the rain, and she catches Tobin by the overalls halfway down and brings him round in a long wobbling curve to land in the middle of the street, in front of everyone. Nobody cheers at first. Then everybody does. The Wattrel flies circles round her head. She is crying. She flew because she wanted to.

effects.text: In a storm, the courier who had lost her flying took a borrowed broom and flew on her own, and caught her friend.

events.intro: Three stages on, a storm hits the town while you are passing through it. The wind is a wall. Up on the clock tower, Tobin is trying to tie down the hands of the clock, and then he is not on the clock tower any more. He is hanging off the edge of it by one arm. The girl is in the street below with her broom. She looks up at him, and at the broom, and at you. Her face is white. The Wattrel is screaming. She has to fly.

success.text: She grits her teeth and kicks off. She flies crooked and terrified, because you told her she could. She catches Tobin by the sleeve as he lets go, and they crash together into the baker's awning, both alive. Later, wrapped in a blanket, she says: "I flew because you said so. I'll need my own reason. But thank you." She gives you an egg from the Wattrel's nest, and cake.

Your Flying-type is up before the girl can move. It takes Tobin by the overalls as his fingers slip and brings him down hard and safe into the street. She runs to him. She does not fly. Later, she thanks you with an egg from the Wattrel's nest and a whole cake, and asks, very quietly, whether you think it will ever come back.

You say nothing. She waits for somebody to tell her she can. Nobody does. She kicks off anyway, and the broom drops like a stone after three metres. The Wattrel goes for Tobin's collar and your lead goes for her, and all of them land in the fountain, soaked and alive. She sits in the water and laughs until she cries. "Not yet," she says. "Not yet." She gives you an egg from the Wattrel's nest, and cake.
